section_summary: This section documents the Department of State's diplomatic correspondence, intelligence coordination, and operational efforts between late September and late October 1945 to locate, impound, and examine Japanese diplomatic and consular archives and assets worldwide following the surrender of Japan. It details inter-Allied negotiations and jurisdictional friction regarding French exclusion from archival seizures in the Levant, coordination among the Big Four powers (United States, Great Britain, Soviet Union, and China), and administrative stalemates stemming from General Douglas MacArthur's delay in issuing formal surrender instructions to Japanese overseas missions. Additionally, the section includes comprehensive intelligence inventories of recovered Japanese records and espionage files from Panama, El Salvador, and Ecuador, as well as high-level diplomatic policy discussions with the British Embassy regarding global archival preservation and examination.

subfiles.about: The French Government protests its exclusion from the Allied seizure of Japanese diplomatic archives and property in the Levant and requests participation.
subfiles.summary: French Aide-Memoire 771: France objects to being excluded as Wadsworth obtained Japanese archives from Beirut's Spanish Consulate with US, British, Soviet and Chinese representatives and plans to sequester Japanese property in Syria and Lebanon; it asks to be associated immediately and for U.S. plans on Japanese assets abroad.
subfiles.title: French Embassy Aide-Mémoire No. 771 on Seizure of Japanese Archives and Property in the Levant

subfiles.about: Department routing slip transmitting the French Embassy aide-mémoire for translation and action.
subfiles.from: Mary Gass (Translating Section, Division of Central Services)
subfiles.summary: Routing slip sends French aide-memoire 771 to Adrian Colquitt for translation; a September 26, 1945 note redirects it to Oscar Straus.
subfiles.title: State Department Routing Slip Regarding French Aide-Mémoire
subfiles.to: Adrian B. Colquitt (NE), redirected to Oscar S. Straus (FC)

subfiles.about: US representative to the Holy See reports the Vatican considers the Japanese Embassy's status unchanged and no surrender orders have been received.
subfiles.summary: Tittmann: the Vatican says Japan's ambassador has no Tokyo instructions on handing over archives and property, and regards the embassy's status as unchanged, as the ambassador saw the Pope on September 25; he requests guidance.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 201 from Vatican City on Status of Japanese Embassy to the Holy See

subfiles.about: Colquitt refers the French aide-mémoire and Levant Japanese property question to Straus for action.
subfiles.summary: Colquitt follows a telephone talk with Straus on sequestering Japanese property in Syria and Lebanon, forwards it for action, and asked Translating to deliver the French aide-memoire to Straus.
subfiles.title: Memorandum from NE to FC on Sequestration of Japanese Property in Syria and Lebanon

subfiles.about: Henderson reports his discussion with French Embassy Counselor Lacoste regarding French exclusion from Japanese property actions in the Levant.
subfiles.summary: Loy Henderson records French Counselor Lacoste presenting Aide-Memoire 771 on Wadsworth's failure to consult France in Syria and Lebanon, stressing broader disposal of Japanese property in neutral states; Henderson promises to look into it.
subfiles.title: Memorandum by Loy W. Henderson on Conversation with French Counselor Lacoste

subfiles.about: Routing slip directing correspondence on Japanese diplomatic archives to Far Eastern Affairs.
subfiles.summary: Routing slip to John Carter Vincent transmitting the FC memorandum and a clipping on diplomatic archives and MacArthur's directives.
subfiles.title: Routing Slip to Far Eastern Affairs Regarding Japanese Archives

subfiles.about: Lyon highlights difficulties caused by General MacArthur's delay in issuing archival surrender directives, enclosing a New York Times article.
subfiles.summary: Lyon says a September 22 Times clipping from Stockholm shows confusion since MacArthur hasn't ordered Japan to surrender archives, as Japan's Swedish legation adds staff; overseas missions seek instructions, and he attaches a draft circular telegram on the delay.
subfiles.title: Memorandum from FC to FE Regarding Japanese Archives with New York Times Clipping

subfiles.about: Ambassador Simmons transmits an inventory receipt for Japanese archives delivered in San Salvador and notes the lack of confidential records.
subfiles.from: John F. Simmons (American Ambassador, San Salvador)
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Simmons reports Japanese archives held by the Spanish Legation in San Salvador since December 1941 went to the U.S. Embassy; no correspondence, codes or personnel lists remained, and an August 27, 1945 receipt lists machines, films, discs, flags, abacuses and books.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 474 from San Salvador on Delivery of Japanese Archives

subfiles.about: Transmittal of Despatch No. 474 from San Salvador to US military intelligence agencies and the FBI.
subfiles.summary: State sends copies of San Salvador Despatch 474 (September 28, 1945) on recovered Japanese archives to Military Intelligence, Naval Intelligence and the FBI.
subfiles.title: State Department Transmittal of Despatch No. 474 from San Salvador
subfiles.to: Military Intelligence Division, Office of Naval Intelligence, Federal Bureau of Investigation

subfiles.about: Straus reviews the policy reasons for excluding France from the Big Four archival seizures outside France, enclosing relevant telegrams.
subfiles.summary: Straus says Wadsworth followed instructions limiting archival seizures to the Big Four, though France was included for Japanese property in France; widening invitations would prompt Dutch and Australian demands, and action stays academic until MacArthur orders Tokyo.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on French Participation in Seizure of Japanese Archives with Attached Telegrams

subfiles.about: Acting Secretary Acheson advises diplomatic missions that instructions on Japanese archives remain delayed due to conditions in Tokyo.
subfiles.summary: Acheson informs all missions the instructions expected in the August 29 circular are still delayed by the Tokyo situation, and they'll be telegraphed as soon as MacArthur issues the surrender directives.
subfiles.title: Circular Telegram to All Diplomatic Missions on Delay in Tokyo Instructions

subfiles.about: Transmittal of Despatch No. 2857 from Panama containing a detailed Japanese archival inventory to intelligence agencies.
subfiles.summary: State sends copies of Panama Despatch 2857 (October 1, 1945), a detailed inventory of recovered Japanese records, to Military Intelligence, Naval Intelligence and the FBI.
subfiles.title: State Department Transmittal of Despatch No. 2857 from Panama
subfiles.to: Military Intelligence Division, Office of Naval Intelligence, Federal Bureau of Investigation

subfiles.about: Donnelly transmits a comprehensive 27-page inventory of surviving Japanese Legation archives, card indexes, marked maps, and propaganda in Panama.
subfiles.from: Walter J. Donnelly (American Chargé d'Affaires a.i., Panama)
subfiles.summary: Walter J. Donnelly transmits a detailed inventory of the former Japanese Legation archives in Panama, supervised by Third Secretary V. Lansing Collins, Jr., with army linguists Sakoda and Nishioki, Embassy staff Pettis and Waters, and Chinese Legation Secretary Dr. Yen Shen Lu. The inventory details fifty empty binding folders, Japanese government gazettes (Kanpo), registers of military reservists and residents, an annotated military map of Panama highlighting Canal approaches and defense sites, and card indexes of hundreds of Japanese nationals. It also surveys extensive pre-war propaganda files and correspondence showing Japanese surveillance of Panamanian politics and US military movements prior to Pearl Harbor.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 2857 from Panama Transmitting Detailed Inventory of Japanese Archives

subfiles.about: Ambassador Norweb reports joint Allied examination of Japanese index cards in Havana and the need for an American Japanese-language expert.
subfiles.summary: Norweb: American, British, Chinese and Soviet missions inspected Japanese index cards in Havana with a Cuban-supplied translator and Chinese help on ideographs; detailed intelligence analysis would need an American specialist in written Japanese.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 631 from Habana Regarding Examination of Japanese Index Cards

subfiles.about: Lyon urges SWNCC action to obtain a directive from MacArthur and attaches a comprehensive global summary of archival status.
subfiles.summary: Lyon highlights the anomalous situation confronting US missions abroad because General MacArthur has failed to order the Japanese Government to surrender diplomatic archives, leaving Japanese diplomats unhindered in neutral capitals and protecting powers without authority to release files. Lyon urges that the State-War-Navy Coordinating Committee (SWNCC) prompt the Joint Chiefs of Staff to issue an immediate directive ordering the recall of Japanese diplomats and the transfer of mission archives to US representatives acting for the Allies. An attached country-by-country survey as of October 2, 1945, details the archival status across dozens of posts from Addis Ababa to Wellington.
subfiles.title: Memorandum from FC to FE Urging SWNCC Directive to MacArthur with Worldwide Status Summary

subfiles.about: Ranken transmits a copy of a British Embassy telegram to London concerning US policy and MacArthur's objections.
subfiles.from: G. R. Ranken (Third Secretary, British Embassy, Washington)
subfiles.summary: G. R. Ranken sends Straus the British Embassy's September 14 telegram: State told MacArthur to order Tokyo to hand archives to the Four Powers, MacArthur objected, and the U.S. might accept mere access if hosts insist on custody.
subfiles.title: British Embassy Compliments Slip Transmitting Telegram on State Department Policy

subfiles.about: The Secretary of State transmits photostatic copies of the Japanese map of Panama to the American Mission in Panama.
subfiles.from: James F. Byrnes (Secretary of State, drafted by FC: PFCherp)
subfiles.summary: Per Panama's Despatch 2918 of October 9, 1945, State sends photostatic copies of the marked Panama map recovered from the former Japanese Legation archives.
subfiles.title: State Department Despatch to Panama Transmitting Copies of Japanese Map
subfiles.to: Officer in Charge of the American Mission, Panama

subfiles.about: Collins requests seven photostatic copies of the marked Japanese map of Panama for military intelligence and Allied legations.
subfiles.from: V. Lansing Collins, Jr. (for Chargé d'Affaires a.i., Panama)
subfiles.summary: Collins requests seven photostats of the marked Panama map from Japanese archives for the Panamanian Government, British and Chinese Legations and U.S. intelligence, whose Canal Department G-2 and 15th Naval District officers want to study its markings.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 2918 from Panama Requesting Copies of Japanese Map for Intelligence

subfiles.about: Straus clarifies to Ranken that US policy insists on full physical custody of Japanese archives rather than mere access.
subfiles.summary: Straus corrects Ranken's impression that the U.S. would accept access alone: policy demands full Four Power custody once MacArthur orders; in Argentina the ambassadors planned to get archives from the Swiss Minister as a fait accompli, and Ranken will ask London for revised instructions.
subfiles.title: Memorandum of Conversation between Oscar Straus and G. R. Ranken on Archival Policy

subfiles.about: MacDonald inquires whether certain Japanese documents have been processed by the War Department and where they are located.
subfiles.from: J. E. MacDonald (Division of Economic Security Controls)
subfiles.summary: J. E. MacDonald says Economic Security Controls wants to know the location and War Department processing status of specified Japanese papers, not immediate possession.
subfiles.title: Memorandum from ES to FC Inquiring About War Department Processing of Japanese Documents

subfiles.about: Straus provides Ranken with the draft text of the JCS message to MacArthur regarding surrender instructions for Japanese archives.
subfiles.summary: Straus tells Ranken the Joint Chiefs asked MacArthur to order Japan to surrender diplomatic archives and property, handing him the proposed directive for neutral, protecting-power and Allied countries; Ranken says it fully resolves London's concerns.
subfiles.title: Memorandum of Conversation between Oscar Straus and G. R. Ranken with JCS Directive Text

subfiles.about: Tittmann reports that his British colleague to the Holy See has now received formal instructions regarding Japanese archives.
subfiles.summary: Tittmann says his British colleague, who had joined demarches on his own responsibility, received London's formal instructions by mail dated October 1 authorizing participation.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 208 from Vatican City on British Instructions Regarding Japanese Archives

subfiles.about: The British Embassy presents a comprehensive plan for Allied preservation, examination, and inter-Allied sharing of Japanese records worldwide.
subfiles.summary: The British Embassy submits a detailed five-page aide-mémoire emphasizing that Allied access to Japanese official and non-official records in Japan and abroad is essential for locating POWs and civilian internees, prosecuting war criminals, controlling disarmament, and identifying assets for reparations. It defines records comprehensively, urges orders forbidding destruction under severe penalties, and proposes that SCAP and theater commanders set up examination organizations. Great Britain requests the inclusion of British, Dominion, and Indian experts in Japan, proposes mechanisms to share intelligence among Allied governments, and asks if the US concurs and will instruct MacArthur accordingly.
subfiles.title: British Embassy Aide-Mémoire on Preservation and Examination of Japanese Records Worldwide

subfiles.about: Circular telegram transmitting the text of the JCS directive to MacArthur regarding instructions for the surrender of Japanese archives.
subfiles.from: James F. Byrnes (Secretary of State, drafted by FC: OSStraus)
subfiles.summary: Byrnes quotes the JCS directive to MacArthur: neutral-state Japanese missions surrender archives to Four Power representatives with protection of nationals left to Sweden or Switzerland; protecting-power countries give Four Powers custody; Allied nations' hosts get custody with Big Four access.
subfiles.title: Circular Telegram to All Diplomatic Missions on JCS Directive to General MacArthur

subfiles.about: Byrnes instructs the Embassy in Buenos Aires to limit Swiss access to archives strictly to routine passport and visa files.
subfiles.from: James F. Byrnes (Secretary of State, drafted by FC: PFCherp)
subfiles.summary: Byrnes tells Buenos Aires Swiss access after transfer must be strictly limited to passport, visa and similar routine files; other procedural questions are covered in the October 13 circular.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 1530 to Buenos Aires on Limiting Swiss Access to Archives

subfiles.about: Byrnes authorizes accepting access rather than custody for archives in Mexico if Allied colleagues agree, or temporary joint Four Power receipt.
subfiles.from: James F. Byrnes (Secretary of State, drafted by FC: PFCherp)
subfiles.summary: Byrnes tells Mexico City access will satisfy State if the British, Soviet, Chinese and Swedish agree; if Sweden insists on transfer and Mexico objects, the U.S. will receive the archives jointly and immediately hand custody to Mexico's Foreign Office.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 1679 to Mexico City on Transfer and Access to Japanese Archives

subfiles.about: Shaw reports that Spain released Japanese Legation property in Quito to Ecuador, notes an unopened safe, and transmits inventories.
subfiles.from: Geo. P. Shaw (Chargé d'Affaires a.i., Quito)
subfiles.summary: Shaw reports Spain's Minister turned Japanese archives and property to Ecuador's Foreign Ministry: routine furnishings, books and two folders, plus an unopened Remington safe whose combination Nagumo withheld; he sends the 1942 inventory and asks whether to demand custody and how to open the safe.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 3560 from Quito on Release of Japanese Archives and Property in Ecuador

subfiles.about: Cabot reports plans to terminate leases on Japanese premises in Belgrano, rent downtown space, intern Chancellor Tani, and manage Swiss access.
subfiles.from: John M. Cabot (Chargé d'Affaires a.i., Buenos Aires)
subfiles.summary: Cabot plans to end leases on the ex-Japanese Belgrano residence and office, rent a downtown office for Allied examination and Swiss access, and have Chancellor Tani interned and replaced by a vetted translator; he asks how much Swiss access is allowed.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 2533 from Buenos Aires on Arrangements for Japanese Archives and Swiss Representation

subfiles.about: Internal note approving the forwarding of Collins's detailed Panama archival report.
subfiles.summary: RPH tells Thomas Mann there's no objection to forwarding Collins's essay and inventory on Japanese archives in Panama.
subfiles.title: Internal Note to Mr. Mann Regarding Forwarding Collins's Panama Inventory

subfiles.about: Straus attaches a copy of the British telegram to London and his memorandum for Clattenburg.
subfiles.summary: Straus sends Albert Clattenburg the British Embassy's telegram on Japanese archives and his memorandum, noting he handled it directly with Ranken.
subfiles.title: Internal Note from Oscar Straus to Albert Clattenburg Regarding British Telegram
